chunks.text: The trans-Saharan trade was the network of caravan routes crossing the Sahara Desert, linking the gold-rich savanna of West Africa to North Africa, the Mediterranean, and the wider Islamic world. The routes were ancient but grew busier and richer between c. 1200 and c. 1450.

In parts of medieval West Africa, salt was traded for gold at close to an even, pound-for-pound exchange. This made sense because West Africa had abundant gold but almost no salt, while the Sahara had salt but no gold, so each region possessed in surplus what the other desperately needed.

Salt was a biological necessity, not a decorative luxury. Human bodies need it to survive, especially in hot climates where sweat drains it away, and it was essential for preserving meat and fish, which is why salt-starved West Africa valued it so highly.

The camel was the vehicle of the trans-Saharan trade, often called the 'ship of the desert.' Camels can go many days without water, tolerate brutal heat, and walk on sand that would bog down a horse or ox, making them the only pack animal able to cross the Sahara.

The camel saddle was the key technology that unlocked large-scale trans-Saharan trade. An effective saddle let camels carry heavy cargo across long distances and be controlled by a rider, enabling traders to organize camels into caravans.

Trans-Saharan traders organized camels into caravans, sometimes thousands of animals traveling together for safety and efficiency. These caravans moved from oasis to oasis, the desert's equivalent of ports, where water and rest could be found.

Gold from the West African goldfields was the prize that drew merchants across the Sahara. It flowed north to North Africa, Egypt, and beyond, where it was minted into coins and became a foundation of Mediterranean and Islamic economies.

Salt mined in the Sahara, at places like the great mining settlement of Taghaza, was carried south in slabs to the salt-starved societies of West Africa. Salt moving south and gold moving north was the defining exchange of the trans-Saharan trade.

Besides gold and salt, trans-Saharan caravans carried ivory, kola nuts, and enslaved people northward, and horses, textiles, manufactured goods, books, copper, and Islam southward. The trans-Saharan slave trade carried enslaved Africans across the desert for centuries.

Like the Silk Roads, the trans-Saharan trade specialized in goods whose high value justified the costly, dangerous journey. Gold, with extraordinary value packed into a small weight, was the ideal trans-Saharan cargo, much as silk was for the overland Asian routes.
Ghana was the first great gold-trading empire of the western Sudan, but it declined before the period c. 1200–1450. It was the predecessor to the later empires of Mali and Songhai.

The Mali Empire, founded by Sundiata around 1235, rose to dominate the western Sudan by controlling and taxing the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade. Its ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 that displayed Mali's enormous wealth.

The Songhai Empire, expanding from its capital at Gao under rulers such as Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad, grew in the 1400s into the largest empire West Africa had ever seen. It was built on control of the trans-Saharan trade.

Trans-Saharan trade built empires through a self-reinforcing cycle: a ruler who controlled key trading cities and protected caravan routes grew rich by taxing gold and salt, used that wealth to build armies, and conquered more territory and routes, generating still more wealth.

Timbuktu, near the Niger River at the crossroads of the gold and salt trades, grew into a thriving commercial center and one of the great intellectual capitals of the Islamic world. Its mosques, schools, and libraries held tens of thousands of manuscripts on law, science, theology, and history.

Gao, the capital of the Songhai Empire, and Djenne, a Niger-region city famous for its great mud-brick mosque, flourished as hubs of commerce and Islamic culture alongside Timbuktu. These cities concentrated the wealth the trans-Saharan trade generated.

Trans-Saharan trade spread Islam into West Africa because the merchants crossing the Sahara were Muslim and the lucrative trade connected the region to the Islamic world. West African rulers had strong incentives to adopt Islam to ease commerce and gain prestige.

Islam took deepest root in West Africa among rulers, merchants, and city-dwellers, while many rural people retained indigenous beliefs, often blending the two. The conversion of West Africa to Islam was uneven and syncretic rather than total.

Across every network in this era, trade routes generated wealth, wealth concentrated in cities at the network's crossroads, and those cities became centers of culture and religion. Timbuktu and Gao on the trans-Saharan routes parallel Samarkand on the Silk Roads and Kilwa and Malacca on the Indian Ocean.

The trans-Saharan trade used the camel and the gold–salt exchange, the Silk Roads used overland camel caravans for luxury goods, and the Indian Ocean used monsoon-driven ships for both bulk and luxury goods. All three spread Islam and built crossroads cities, but each had a distinctive vehicle and signature goods.

So much West African gold flowed north across the Sahara that it became a backbone of Mediterranean and Islamic economies and was minted into coins used from Cairo to Italy. This wealth later motivated Europeans to reach the source of African gold directly by sailing down the African coast.

The Songhai Empire fell in 1591 to an invading army from Morocco that won largely because it carried gunpowder firearms the Songhai lacked. This previews the rise of gunpowder as the decisive military technology of the early modern world.
